track.title: Stardust
track.album: Stardust / One Night in Havana (Gennett 78 rpm single)
track.query: Hoagy Carmichael and His Pals Stardust 1927 Gennett
track.notes: The 31 Oct 1927 Gennett instrumental by Hoagy Carmichael and His Pals (6311), not Louis Armstrong's 1931 or Artie Shaw's 1940 versions

notes: Date, studio, release number 6311, personnel and the 3:02 length all from the Wikipedia article; the infobox gives release in October 1928. Wikipedia says the session was booked for 31 Oct 1927. Grammy Hall of Fame 1995 for this recording; the Armstrong (1931) and Shaw (1940) versions are separate Hall of Fame entries.

title: Pine Top's Boogie Woogie
original_issue: Vocalion (78 rpm single), released 1 March 1929; catalogue number not verified
personnel: Pine Top Smith (piano, vocal)
trivia: This is the first known recording of a song with "boogie" in its title, and its words are instructions to the dancers. Smith died from a gunshot wound in a Chicago dance-hall fight in March 1929, the day before a scheduled second Vocalion session.

track.title: Pine Top's Boogie Woogie
track.album: Pine Top's Boogie Woogie (Vocalion 78 rpm single)
track.query: Pine Top Smith Pine Top's Boogie Woogie 1928 Vocalion
track.notes: Pine Top Smith's December 1928 Vocalion original, not later versions such as Tommy Dorsey's 1938 recording

notes: Recording date (Chicago), release date (1 Mar 1929), Vocalion label and the 3:08 length are from the Wikipedia infobox; no Vocalion catalogue number was found in the sources read, hence medium. The Grammy Hall of Fame (inducted 1983) lists it as Jazz; boogie-woogie piano is jazz-adjacent. Title spelling varies (Pinetop's / Pine Top's / Pine-Top's).

title: Apex Blues
original_issue: Vocalion 2779 (78 rpm); also Brunswick 4966 and Brunswick 7096
personnel: Jimmie Noone (clarinet, leader) with his Apex Club Orchestra quintet; sidemen for this session not verified (see notes)
trivia: Noone's Apex Club band, a quintet with clarinet and alto sax but no brass, was unusual for the time, and the Chicago club was raided and shut down in 1929. Excerpts of Apex Blues were played in the 1944 East Side Kids film Block Busters.

track.title: Apex Blues
track.album: Apex Blues (Vocalion 78 rpm single)
track.query: Jimmie Noone Apex Club Orchestra Apex Blues 1929 Vocalion
track.notes: The July 1929 Vocalion recording by Noone's Apex Club band (2779), not later Noone performances such as the one heard in Block Busters

notes: Date 11 July 1929, Chicago, Vocalion 2779 and the Brunswick reissue numbers from the Red Hot Jazz list; no source read lists the sidemen for this exact session. Wikipedia names the regular Apex Club group as Joe Poston (alto sax), Earl Hines (piano), Bud Scott (banjo, guitar) and Johnny Wells (drums, from 1928), and the Red Hot Jazz roster also lists Alex Hill among the band's pianists, so none is claimed for this date. Release year 1929 is assumed, not verified. Duration is a generic 78 rpm length, not read from a source.

title: Jazz Battle
original_issue: Brunswick 4244 (78 rpm)
personnel: Jabbo Smith (trumpet, vocal) and His Rhythm Aces; sidemen for this session not verified (see notes)
trivia: Jabbo Smith recorded 20 sides for Brunswick in 1929 (19 were issued) and was billed as a rival to Louis Armstrong. Most of the records did not sell well enough for Brunswick to extend his contract.

track.title: Jazz Battle

The Red Hot Jazz roster for the whole series lists Omer Simeon, Willard Brown and George James (reeds), Cassino Simpson and Earl Frazier (piano), Ikey Robinson (banjo), Hayes Alvis and Lawson Buford (tuba) but does not map them to dates, so no sidemen are credited. Release year assumed 1929. Duration is a generic 78 rpm length, not read from a source.

title: My Blue Heaven
original_issue: Victor 20964 (78 rpm, b/w Are You Thinking of Me To-night?), matrix BVE-39179, released November 1927
personnel: Gene Austin (vocal) with the Victor Orchestra directed by Nat Shilkret; individual players not verified
trivia: Austin gave Victor an ultimatum that he would record no more unless this song was issued, and the record went on to sell more than five million copies. In Austin's own later account, the studio players left before the take and he recorded it with an improvised backing of a cellist, a pianist and a whistler.

track.title: My Blue Heaven
track.album: My Blue Heaven / Are You Thinking of Me To-night? (Victor 78 rpm single)
track.query: Gene Austin My Blue Heaven 1927 Victor
track.notes: Gene Austin's Victor 20964 recording of September 1927 (the Grammy Hall of Fame record), not the Paul Whiteman, Bing Crosby, Fats Domino or later versions

notes: Recording date (14 Sept 1927, Victor Studios, New York), Victor 20964, matrix BVE-39179 (from the title of the UCSB Victor discography page cited by Wikipedia; that page itself could not be fetched), B-side and the 4 Nov 1927 release date (from a Discogs citation in Wikipedia) are as given in the Wikipedia article. Wikipedia also says the song became a huge hit in 1928; release year 1927 follows the infobox. Grammy Hall of Fame 1978 per the Hall of Fame list (Traditional pop, 1927 single). Conflict in accompaniment: the article credits the Victor Orchestra under Nat Shilkret, while Austin's own recollection quoted there describes a makeshift cello, piano and whistle trio; the orchestra credit is used and the anecdote is attributed to Austin. Duration 3:35 is a MusicBrainz compilation-track length (215 s); reissue lengths range from about 3:34 to 3:42. Crossover pop-vocal pick from the jazz age.

title: Honky Tonk Train Blues
original_issue: Paramount (78 rpm, b/w Whistlin' Blues), released 1929; catalogue number not verified
personnel: Meade Lux Lewis (piano, solo)
trivia: Lewis's recording debut imitates a train in rolling boogie-woogie piano and is described as the first recorded use of the word honky-tonk in a song. It sold poorly at first, and Lewis was working in a car wash when John Hammond tracked him down and had him record it again in 1935 and 1937.

track.title: Honky Tonk Train Blues
track.album: Honky Tonk Train Blues / Whistlin' Blues (Paramount 78 rpm single)
track.query: Meade Lux Lewis Honky Tonk Train Blues 1927 Paramount original version
track.notes: The 1927 Paramount original (issued 1929), not Lewis's remakes for Parlophone (1935) and Victor (1937) or later versions such as Bob Crosby/Bob Zurke's 1938 big-band record

notes: GAP: recorded 1927, first released 1929 (2 yrs). The Wikipedia infobox gives recorded 1927, released 1929 on Paramount (b/w Whistlin' Blues, 3:10). The month December 1927 comes only from the MusicBrainz recording relation for the Smithsonian Jazz Piano track (2:49 on that CD; other MusicBrainz copies run about 3:10-3:13, the 3:10 of the Wikipedia infobox is used), so the day and the Paramount catalogue number are not verified, hence medium. Wikipedia and the Meade Lux Lewis article say the 1927 recording was his debut, the Parlophone remake is 1935 and the Victor remake 1937. The recording location is not stated in the articles read. Wikipedia reports the original was inducted into the Blues Hall of Fame in 2026. Boogie-woogie piano filed under style chicago, like the Pine Top Smith card.
